questions.question: What three topics does chapter 11 say it covers?
questions.answer: The branches of computer vision (image classification, image segmentation, object detection), building a segmentation model from scratch, and using the pretrained Segment Anything Model.
questions.explanation: Taken from the 'This chapter covers' box on the page.

questions.question: How does the book summarize what an image classification model does?
options: An image goes in, a label comes out
An image goes in, a mask the size of the image comes out
An image goes in, a list of bounding boxes comes out
A label goes in, an image comes out
questions.answer: An image goes in, a label comes out
questions.explanation: Quoted from p332_e11. A mask is the output of segmentation, boxes are the output of detection, and label-to-image is generation (chapter 17).

questions.question: Which use case did chapter 8 use to introduce deep learning for computer vision?
questions.answer: Binary image classification (dogs versus cats).
questions.explanation: p332_e09 says 'binary image classification'. The dogs-vs-cats dataset is the chapter 8 example.

questions.question: Why might the authors begin a segmentation chapter by surveying several vision tasks rather than going straight to segmentation?
questions.answer: Comparing tasks by what they output (a label, a per-pixel mask, labeled boxes) shows what is new about segmentation and helps you choose the right formulation for a problem. For example, detection is cheaper when pixel precision is not needed (p.354).
questions.explanation: This is an interpretation of the chapter structure. The page itself only states that classification is one of three essential tasks.

questions.question: Before turning the page, can you guess what the outputs of segmentation and object detection look like, compared with classification?
questions.answer: Self-check: segmentation outputs a class for every pixel (a mask the size of the image), and detection outputs bounding boxes, each with a class. Compare with p.333.
questions.explanation: Checks readiness for section 11.1.

questions.question: In figure 11.1, which panel uses checkboxes with Bike, Person, and Tree ticked?
questions.answer: Multi-label classification
questions.explanation: Checkboxes mean several labels can apply at once. The single-label panel uses radio buttons (Biking). The segmentation panel uses colored masks, and the detection panel uses rectangles.

questions.question: What is the difference between single-label and multilabel classification, according to the page?
questions.answer: In single-label classification the categories are mutually exclusive, so the image gets exactly one. In multilabel classification you tag all categories the image belongs to.
questions.explanation: Stated in p333_e03.

questions.question: Which application does the book use to illustrate image segmentation?
options: Custom backgrounds in Zoom or Google Meet video calls
Monitoring cars, pedestrians, and signs from a self-driving car
Estimating how visually similar two images are
questions.answer: Custom backgrounds in Zoom or Google Meet video calls
questions.explanation: The book's segmentation example separates you from your background with pixel-level precision. Google Photos illustrates multilabel classification, self-driving cars illustrate detection, and similarity scoring is a niche task listed on p.334.

questions.question: For each of the following, which task fits best, and why? (a) counting pedestrians crossing a street, (b) measuring the area of a tumor in a medical scan, (c) tagging vacation photos with keywords.
questions.answer: (a) Object detection: counting needs individual instances, not exact shapes, and detection is cheaper. (b) Segmentation: area needs the exact outline at pixel level. (c) Multilabel classification: you need all applicable tags for the whole image, with no location.
questions.explanation: Applies the definitions on this page. The counting example matches p.353-354, where detection is preferred when pixel-level information is not needed.

questions.question: In figure 11.1 both riders share the same color in the segmentation panel, but the detection panel draws two separate 'person' boxes. What does this tell you about the two outputs?
questions.answer: The segmentation shown is semantic: it labels pixels by category only, so the two people merge into one 'person' class. Detection outputs one box per instance, so it separates individuals but only gives rough rectangles rather than shapes.
questions.explanation: This prepares the semantic vs instance distinction on p.334.

questions.question: How many classes does the book say the Google Photos multilabel model has, and what is it trained on?
questions.answer: Over 20,000 classes, trained on millions of images.
questions.explanation: Stated in p333_e03.

questions.question: Can you sketch, for one photo of your choice, what a single-label, multilabel, segmentation, and detection output would look like?
questions.answer: Self-check: you should produce one exclusive label, a set of ticked labels, a per-pixel colored mask, and a set of labeled rectangles, as in figure 11.1.
questions.explanation: Reproducing figure 11.1 on a new image checks that you understand all four formats.

questions.question: An image contains two cats. Which segmentation type maps all their pixels to the same generic 'cat' category?
questions.answer: Semantic segmentation
questions.explanation: This is exactly the book's definition of semantic segmentation. Instance segmentation separates cat 1 and cat 2, panoptic gives both labels, and keypoint detection is not segmentation.

questions.question: Which segmentation type does the book call the most informative, and why?
questions.answer: Panoptic segmentation, because it assigns each pixel both a semantic label (like 'cat') and an instance label (like 'cat 2').
questions.explanation: Stated in p334_e10.

questions.question: List at least three of the 'more niche' computer vision tasks the page mentions.
questions.answer: Any three of: image similarity scoring, keypoint detection, pose estimation, 3D mesh estimation, depth estimation.
questions.explanation: From p334_e03.

questions.question: Looking at figure 11.2, what can you do with the right panel that you cannot do with the left?
questions.answer: Count the cats (four) and outline or measure each cat individually. The left (semantic) panel merges all cats into one 'cat' region.
questions.explanation: Instance segmentation parses out individual object instances; semantic segmentation does not.

questions.question: A 10 × 10 image has three classes (background, cat, dog). What is the shape of a semantic segmentation model's probability output, and how many independent per-pixel decisions does it make?
questions.answer: (10, 10, 3): a 3-way class distribution at each pixel, so 100 per-pixel classification decisions.
questions.explanation: This follows from the definition 'assign a class to each pixel'. The output layout is beyond the book on this page but matches section 11.2's approach.

questions.question: Which statement reflects the book's plan for chapters 11 and 12?
options: Chapter 11 covers image segmentation, and object detection is covered in detail in the next chapter
Chapter 11 covers segmentation and detection together
Chapter 11 revisits classification in detail before segmentation
questions.answer: Chapter 11 covers image segmentation, and object detection is covered in detail in the next chapter
questions.explanation: Stated in p334_e04. Classification was covered in chapter 8, and section 11.2 focuses on semantic segmentation (p.335), not panoptic.

questions.question: For a self-driving car that must avoid each individual pedestrian and know which pixels are drivable road, which segmentation type would you choose and why?
questions.answer: Self-check: panoptic. It labels road pixels semantically and separates pedestrians as individual instances.
questions.explanation: Applies the three definitions. Autonomous driving is one of the applications the page lists.

questions.question: What does a pixel value of 3 mean in an Oxford-IIIT Pets mask?
questions.answer: Contour
questions.explanation: The page lists 1 (foreground), 2 (background), 3 (contour). Species is not encoded in the mask.

questions.question: How does the book define a segmentation mask?
questions.answer: The image segmentation equivalent of a label: an image the same size as the input image, with a single color channel, where each integer value corresponds to the class of the corresponding input pixel.
questions.explanation: Quoted almost verbatim from p335_e07.

questions.question: Why does the code use the glob pattern "[!.]*.png" for the masks?
options: To ignore spurious files in the trimaps directory whose names start with a '.'
To select only masks of cats rather than dogs
To exclude masks that contain the contour class
To sort the files by breed
questions.answer: To ignore spurious files in the trimaps directory whose names start with a '.'
questions.explanation: The callout says exactly this. The pattern does not look at species or mask contents, and sorting is done by sorted(), not by the pattern.

questions.question: Why are both path lists passed through sorted(), and what would go wrong without it?
questions.answer: Inputs and masks share filenames, so sorting both lists puts matching pairs at the same index. Without sorting, glob's filesystem-dependent order could pair images with the wrong masks, and the model would train on incorrect targets without any error.
questions.explanation: This follows from p335_e13 (same name in both folders) and the code in p335_e15.

questions.question: The input images are JPG but the masks are PNG. Why is that a sensible choice for masks?
questions.answer: PNG is lossless, so integer class values (1, 2, 3) are stored exactly. JPEG's lossy compression would create intermediate or invalid values near boundaries and corrupt the labels.
questions.explanation: Beyond the book's text, but it follows from the definition of a mask as a grid of exact integer class ids.

questions.question: What is the learning goal of the first segmentation example, and which flavor of segmentation is it?
questions.answer: To tell apart the main subject (the pet) and its background in pictures of cats and dogs. It is semantic segmentation.
questions.explanation: Stated in p335_e05.

questions.question: Could you write a one-line check that confirms input_img_paths and target_paths are aligned?
questions.answer: Self-check, for example: `all(a.stem == b.stem for a, b in zip(input_img_paths, target_paths)) and len(input_img_paths) == len(target_paths)`.
questions.explanation: Comparing filename stems directly checks the pairing the code relies on.

questions.question: After display_target's transformation, what value does a contour pixel have?
questions.explanation: Contour is label 3: (3 - 1) × 127 = 254. 0 is foreground (label 1), 127 is background (label 2), and 255 never occurs because the scale factor is 127.

questions.question: Why does the code pass color_mode="grayscale" when loading the mask?
questions.answer: So the mask is treated as having a single color channel (one class id per pixel), giving an array of shape (H, W, 1).
questions.explanation: The callout says exactly this; a mask is defined on p.335 as a single-channel image.

questions.question: Why is the multiplier 127 and not 128?
questions.answer: The largest shifted label is 2; 2 × 128 = 256 overflows uint8 (wraps to 0), whereas 2 × 127 = 254 fits.
questions.explanation: The array is cast to uint8 (range 0–255) before the arithmetic, so the result must stay ≤ 255.

questions.question: What would you see if you displayed the raw mask (values 1–3) on a 0–255 grayscale scale, and why?
questions.answer: An almost uniformly black image, because 1, 2 and 3 are barely above 0 on a 0–255 scale.
questions.explanation: This is why the authors rescale labels before display.

questions.question: Why does display_target index normalized_array[:, :, 0]?
questions.answer: To drop the trailing channel axis of size 1 and pass a 2-D (H, W) array to plt.imshow.
questions.explanation: img_to_array returns shape (H, W, 1); imshow accepts 2-D arrays or arrays with 3 or 4 channels.

questions.question: Can you explain how you know that target_paths[9] is the mask of input_img_paths[9]?
questions.answer: Both lists were built by sorting filenames that share the same stem (e.g. Abyssinian_1.jpg / Abyssinian_1.png), so equal indices refer to the same picture.
questions.explanation: See the path-list construction on p.335.

questions.question: Why does the code create a new random.Random(1337) for each shuffle?
options: So both lists receive the same permutation and stay aligned
To shuffle the masks differently from the images
questions.answer: So both lists receive the same permutation and stay aligned
questions.explanation: The callout says the same seed keeps input and target paths in the same order. Speed is irrelevant, random.shuffle works on any list, and shuffling them differently would destroy the pairing.

questions.question: Why were the paths shuffled at all?
questions.answer: They were originally sorted by breed; shuffling ensures the later train/validation split is random rather than breed-based.
questions.explanation: Callout plus the split on p.338, which takes the last 1,000 samples.

questions.question: What shape and dtype does path_to_target return?
questions.answer: A uint8 array of shape (200, 200, 1) with values 0, 1, 2.
questions.explanation: Grayscale load at img_size gives one channel; astype("uint8") - 1 sets dtype and shifts labels.

questions.question: Why must the labels start at 0 rather than 1?
questions.answer: Because they index the model's per-pixel softmax output with num_classes=3 entries (indices 0, 1, 2); sparse cross-entropy uses the label as an index.
questions.explanation: With labels 1–3, label 3 would be out of range.

questions.question: A mask row reads [3, 1, 1, 2]. What does path_to_target turn it into?
questions.explanation: Subtract 1 from each value.

questions.question: In figure 11.4, which colour corresponds to the contour class, and why does it appear as a thick band?
questions.answer: Yellow (highest value, 254). The contour class marks the uncertain boundary region around the pet, which annotators drew as a band several pixels wide.
questions.explanation: Viridis maps the largest value to yellow; the contour is label 3, the highest.

questions.question: Could you rewrite the alignment-preserving shuffle using a single NumPy permutation applied to both lists?
questions.answer: Yes: perm = np.random.default_rng(1337).permutation(n); then index both lists with perm.
questions.explanation: Any method that applies one permutation to both lists preserves pairing.

questions.question: What is the shape of x right after the six Conv2D layers?
questions.explanation: Three stride-2 layers halve 200 three times: 100, 50, 25; the last layers have 256 filters. (100,100,64) and (50,50,128) are intermediate shapes; 12 would need a fourth stride.

questions.question: Why is the targets array uint8 with one channel while input_imgs is float32 with three?
questions.answer: Targets hold one integer class label per pixel; inputs hold RGB values that will be processed as floats.
questions.explanation: From the callout on the loading loop.

questions.question: Without padding="same" (i.e. with 'valid' padding and stride 1), what would a 3 × 3 Conv2D do to a 100 × 100 feature map, and why is that a problem here?
questions.answer: It would produce 98 × 98; the shrinkage accumulates, so the decoder would not end exactly at 200 × 200 to match the masks.
questions.explanation: Valid output size = H − k + 1 = 100 − 3 + 1 = 98. The callout says padding='same' avoids border effects on feature-map size.

questions.question: What does input_imgs[:-num_val_samples] select?
questions.answer: All samples except the last 1,000, which become the training inputs.
questions.explanation: Negative slicing; the complementary slice [-1000:] is the validation set.

questions.question: Why must the model's final spatial size equal the input's?
questions.answer: Because the loss compares a prediction for every pixel with the 200 × 200 mask; the output must provide one class distribution per mask pixel.
questions.explanation: That is the motivation for the Conv2DTranspose decoder explained on p.339.

questions.question: What is the purpose of Rescaling(1.0 / 255)?
options: Normalize each image to zero mean
questions.answer: Map pixel values from [0, 255] to [0, 1]
questions.explanation: The callout says rescale input images to the [0–1] range. Resizing was done by load_img, labels are untouched, and no mean subtraction is performed.

questions.question: Can you write down the shape after each of the 12 hidden layers without looking?
questions.explanation: Halve at each strided Conv2D, double at each strided Conv2DTranspose; channels = filters.

questions.question: Why does this segmentation model avoid MaxPooling2D?
options: Max pooling has too many parameters
Max pooling discards which location in each window produced the value
Max pooling cannot be used with padding="same"
Max pooling only works on grayscale images
questions.answer: Max pooling discards which location in each window produced the value
questions.explanation: The book's argument: one scalar per window with zero knowledge of its location. Pooling has no parameters, works with any padding and any number of channels.

questions.question: What is the output shape of Conv2DTranspose(32, 3, strides=2, padding="same") applied to a (25, 25, 256) tensor?
questions.explanation: Stride 2 doubles the spatial size; the channel count equals the number of filters.

questions.question: What does the final layer Conv2D(num_classes, 3, activation="softmax", padding="same") produce?
questions.answer: A (200, 200, 3) tensor: for every pixel, a probability distribution over the three classes.
questions.explanation: Callout: per-pixel three-way softmax.

questions.question: In what sense is the encoder a 'kind of compression'?
questions.answer: It maps 200 × 200 × 3 = 120,000 values to 25 × 25 × 256 = 160,000 values with far fewer spatial positions (625 instead of 40,000); each position summarizes a large chunk of the image.
questions.explanation: The compression is spatial: the information is moved from spatial extent into channels. (The raw value count actually grows slightly.)

questions.question: Is Conv2DTranspose the inverse of Conv2D? Explain.
questions.answer: Only for shapes: it undoes the spatial downsampling of a matching strided Conv2D, but it has its own learned weights and does not recover the original values.
questions.explanation: The book calls it a kind of inverse that learns to upsample, and gives the shape example.

questions.question: Which other models in the book does this page say also prefer strides over max pooling?
questions.answer: Generative models in chapter 17
questions.explanation: The page cites chapter 17's generative models as location-sensitive. The other options are not mentioned.

questions.question: Can you explain to someone why a classifier can afford to lose location information but a segmenter cannot?
questions.answer: A classifier only needs to know whether a feature is present anywhere; a segmenter must output a label for each pixel, so it needs to know where features are.
questions.explanation: This is the core argument of the page.

questions.question: A true foreground region has 500 pixels, the predicted one has 600, and they overlap on 400. What is the IoU?
questions.explanation: Union = |P| + |G| − |P ∩ G|.

questions.question: Why is sparse_y_pred set to False?
options: Because the model outputs dense softmax probabilities per class
To compute IoU over all classes
questions.answer: Because the model outputs dense softmax probabilities per class
questions.explanation: Callout: our model's predictions are a dense softmax. Targets are integers (sparse_y_true=True), the flag has nothing to do with sparse tensors, and target_class_ids controls which classes are evaluated.

questions.question: What does target_class_ids=(0,) select and why 0?
questions.answer: IoU is computed only for class 0, which is the foreground (the pet) after the labels were shifted from 1–3 to 0–2.
questions.explanation: See the callout and p.337.

questions.question: Why does IoU penalize a model that labels every pixel as foreground?
questions.answer: The intersection becomes the whole true region, but the union becomes the whole image, so the ratio equals the fraction of the image that is foreground, typically small.
questions.explanation: The 'extra bits your model might have included by mistake' inflate the union.

questions.question: Which loss is used and why does it fit the data format?
questions.answer: sparse_categorical_crossentropy, because targets are integer class ids per pixel and the outputs are per-pixel softmax distributions.
questions.explanation: No one-hot encoding is required.

questions.question: What does ModelCheckpoint(..., save_best_only=True) do here?
options: Stops training when validation loss rises
Saves the model after every epoch
Saves the model only when validation loss improves
questions.answer: Saves the model only when validation loss improves
questions.explanation: save_best_only keeps the best monitored value (val_loss by default). Stopping is EarlyStopping; saving every epoch is save_best_only=False; the whole model is saved, not just optimizer state.

questions.question: Can you list the three steps of computing IoU and give its range?
questions.answer: Intersection, union, divide; range 0 to 1.
questions.explanation: Directly from the numbered list.

questions.question: In figure 11.5, what indicates overfitting?
options: Training loss decreasing while validation loss increases
Validation loss lower than training loss at epoch 1
questions.answer: Training loss decreasing while validation loss increases
questions.explanation: Divergence of the curves is the signature of overfitting. Both decreasing means it is still learning; rising training loss would signal an optimization problem; the epoch-1 ordering is irrelevant.

questions.question: Which model is loaded by keras.models.load_model("oxford_segmentation.keras")?
questions.answer: The model from the epoch with the lowest validation loss, saved by ModelCheckpoint(save_best_only=True).
questions.explanation: The text says we reload our best-performing model according to validation loss.

questions.question: What do 'r--' and 'b' mean in the plotting code?
questions.answer: Red dashed line and solid blue line.
questions.explanation: Matplotlib format strings: color letter + line style.

questions.question: Why is validation_data needed for the checkpoint callback to work as intended?
questions.answer: save_best_only monitors val_loss, which only exists if validation data is evaluated each epoch.
questions.explanation: Without it there is no val_loss to compare.

questions.question: Looking at figure 11.5 yourself, roughly where is the validation loss lowest, and how does that compare to the authors' 'around epoch 25'?
questions.answer: Around epochs 18–20 (about 0.36); by epoch 25 it is already rising (about 0.45). The authors' figure is a rough 'midway' estimate.
questions.explanation: Read from the plot; the checkpoint would pick the actual minimum.

questions.question: Roughly how many gradient steps does each epoch take?
questions.answer: About 100 (≈6,390 training samples / 64).
questions.explanation: 7,390 total − 1,000 validation ≈ 6,390, divided by batch size 64 ≈ 99.8, rounded up to 100.

questions.question: Could you name two techniques that might delay the onset of overfitting in this model?
questions.answer: For example: data augmentation applied jointly to images and masks, dropout/weight decay, or using a pretrained encoder.
questions.explanation: Standard regularization approaches from earlier chapters.

questions.question: What is the shape of `mask` right after `mask = model.predict(np.expand_dims(test_image, 0))[0]`?
questions.explanation: The model outputs (batch, 200, 200, num_classes) = (1, 200, 200, 3); `[0]` removes the batch axis. (200, 200) appears only after argmax; (1, 200, 200, 3) is before indexing; Keras puts channels last, not first.

questions.question: Why does `display_mask` multiply the argmax result by 127?
questions.answer: To map the class indices 0, 1, 2 to 0, 127, 254 so that they are spread across the 0–255 range and are visually distinct, as with the ground-truth masks.
questions.explanation: The same scaling is applied to the targets on p.336. Beyond the book: `plt.imshow` would auto-scale anyway, but the scaling matters for 8-bit image display.

questions.question: In Figure 11.6, which class does the yellow band around the dog represent?
questions.answer: Contour
questions.explanation: Class 2 (contour) becomes 254 after scaling, which viridis renders as yellow. The pet (class 0) is purple and the background (class 1) teal. The artifacts are small stray regions, not the outline.

questions.question: The authors attribute small artifacts to geometric shapes in the image. Why might a per-pixel classifier produce isolated wrong blobs?
questions.answer: Each pixel is classified from local features within its receptive field; edges or textures in the background can resemble pet or contour features, and nothing in the model forces the prediction to be one connected region.
questions.explanation: The page states the cause briefly; the explanation about receptive fields and lack of connectivity constraints is an added interpretation.

questions.question: Give three facts about SAM stated on this page.
questions.answer: Developed by Meta AI; released in April 2023; trained on 11 million images and their masks covering over 1 billion object instances.
questions.explanation: All three appear in the SAM paragraph; the footnote cites Kirillov et al., "Segment Anything" (ICCV 2023).

questions.question: A pixel's predicted probabilities are [0.30, 0.45, 0.25]. What value does `display_mask` assign to it, and what class is that?
questions.answer: argmax = 1, so 1 × 127 = 127: background (teal).
questions.explanation: argmax over the last axis returns the index of the largest probability (0.45 at index 1); the scaling multiplies it by 127.

questions.question: Can you explain, without looking, why section 11.3 switches to a pretrained model even though the from-scratch model 'appears to work nicely'?
questions.answer: Pretrained models trained on huge data (SAM: 11M images, 1B+ masks) give much more general and accurate segmentations than a small model trained on ~7k images, just as pretrained ConvNets helped classification in chapter 8.
questions.explanation: Check that you mention both the chapter 8 parallel and the scale of SAM's training data.

questions.question: According to the page, what is SAM's main innovation?
options: It uses max pooling instead of strided convolutions
It is not limited to a predefined set of object classes
It has more output classes than any other model
It works only after fine-tuning on your data
questions.answer: It is not limited to a predefined set of object classes
questions.explanation: The page says this directly. Pooling is unrelated (and discouraged for segmentation, p.339); SAM doesn't use a fixed list of classes at all; and no fine-tuning is needed.

questions.question: What do the three parts of the preset name `sam_huge_sa1b` stand for?
questions.answer: `sam`: the Segment Anything Model; `huge`: its size (number of parameters); `sa1b`: the SA-1B dataset with 1 billion annotated masks.
questions.explanation: Stated in the paragraph introducing `ImageSegmenter`.

questions.question: Which KerasHub class is used to wrap SAM?
questions.answer: ImageSegmenter
questions.explanation: `ImageSegmenter` is the segmentation task. `ImageClassifier` was used for classification (p.324), a backbone is a feature extractor without a head (p.282), and `ImageConverter` handles image preprocessing (p.282).

questions.question: Explain what it means that SA-1B and SAM were "developed together in a feedback loop." Why was this necessary?
questions.answer: A partially trained SAM was used to help label new images, and humans corrected its output; the improved data trained a better model, which labeled more data. This was necessary because labeling 1 billion masks by hand is infeasible.
questions.explanation: The page describes the model assisting with labeling and increasingly automated collection; the infeasibility argument is an inference from the scale.

questions.question: Check the book's figures: with ~11 million images and ~1 billion masks, how many masks per image is that on average? Is it consistent with "~100 masks on average"?
questions.answer: About $10^9 / 1.1\times10^7 \approx 91$ masks per image, which is consistent with ~100.
questions.explanation: Simple division of the totals from pp.342–343; 'over 1 billion' masks pushes it a bit higher.

questions.question: How many parameters does `model.count_params()` report, and roughly how much memory do the weights take in float32?
questions.answer: 641,090,864 parameters; about 641M × 4 bytes ≈ 2.6 GB.
questions.explanation: The count is printed on the page; the memory estimate is added arithmetic (not in the book).

questions.question: Can you list how using SAM differs from the chapter 8 transfer-learning recipe (feature extraction + new classifier head)?
questions.answer: Chapter 8 reused a pretrained backbone but trained a new head for fixed classes; SAM is used as is, with no new head and no training, and the target is specified by a prompt.
questions.explanation: Compare p.280–282 with this page's 'You don't even need to fine-tune the model first.'

questions.question: In SAM's training triples (image, prompt, mask), which elements are model inputs?
questions.answer: image and prompt
questions.explanation: The page states that image and prompt are the inputs; mask is the ground-truth label used for comparison. 'image only' leaves out the prompt; including mask as input would give away the answer.

questions.question: Name the two prompt forms described on this page.
questions.answer: A point inside the object to mask, and a box around the object to mask.
questions.explanation: These are the two bullets. (The chapter summary on p.352 mentions more prompt types.)

questions.question: Which component takes both the image embedding and the prompt embedding as input?
questions.answer: Mask decoder
questions.explanation: The mask decoder combines both embeddings and outputs candidate masks. The image encoder sees only the image, the prompt encoder only the prompt, and `ImageConverter` is a KerasHub preprocessing layer (p.282).

questions.question: Why is it useful that the mask decoder outputs a few possible masks rather than one?
questions.answer: A prompt can be ambiguous (a point may lie on a part, an object, or a group of objects); several candidates with scores can cover the different valid interpretations instead of averaging them.
questions.explanation: The page states that several masks are output; the ambiguity rationale is an added explanation, consistent with the scores shown in Figure 11.8.

questions.question: Describe the semiautomated stage of SA-1B collection and why it speeds up labeling.
questions.answer: SAM first segments the images; humans then correct its masks and add missing annotations. Editing a draft is much faster than drawing every mask by hand.
questions.explanation: The first sentence of the page describes the stage; the speed argument is an inference.

questions.question: What does the image encoder output, and which earlier model do the authors compare it to?
questions.answer: A much smaller image embedding; they compare it to the Xception model used in previous chapters.
questions.explanation: Stated on the page. Note: the original SAM uses a Vision Transformer, so the comparison is about function.

questions.question: Without looking, sketch SAM's three components and draw the arrows between them, the image, the prompt and the outputs.
questions.answer: image → image encoder → embedding; prompt → prompt encoder → embedding; both → mask decoder → several masks (with scores) compared to the ground truth.
questions.explanation: Compare your sketch with Figure 11.8 on p.345.

questions.question: How is a point prompt created during SAM training, according to the page?
options: A human annotator clicks the object center
A random pixel inside the chosen mask label
The corner of the mask's bounding box
questions.answer: A random pixel inside the chosen mask label
questions.explanation: The page says: 'To create a point prompt, choose a random pixel inside the mask label.' Prompts are not stored human clicks, the image center may not be on the object, and box corners are often outside the object.

questions.question: How is a box prompt created from a mask?
questions.answer: By drawing a box around all points inside the mask label (its bounding box).
questions.explanation: Directly stated on the page.

questions.question: A mask's pixels span columns 120–260 and rows 80–190. What is the box prompt in (x_min, y_min, x_max, y_max) form?
questions.explanation: The box around all mask points is given by the min and max of the column and row coordinates. The coordinate ordering is a common convention, not one the book specifies here.

questions.question: Why can the triple-sampling process be 'repeated indefinitely' on a finite dataset?
questions.answer: Each image has many masks, and each mask allows many different point prompts (any interior pixel), so random sampling keeps producing new (image, prompt, mask) combinations.
questions.explanation: Combines the page's recipe with the ~100 masks per image from p.343.

questions.question: Why does the code call `image_array.astype("uint8")` before `plt.imshow`?
options: `img_to_array` returns float32 in 0–255, which imshow would clip as if the range were [0, 1]
questions.answer: `img_to_array` returns float32 in 0–255, which imshow would clip as if the range were [0, 1]
questions.explanation: Matplotlib reads floats as [0, 1] and integers as [0, 255]. The cast changes neither the resolution nor the number of channels, and has nothing to do with SAM's input format.

questions.question: In Figure 11.8, how many candidate masks does the mask decoder output, and what accompanies each?
questions.answer: Three, each with a score.
questions.explanation: The figure shows three output images, each labelled ', score'.

questions.question: Can you explain why the prompt types SAM accepts at inference time are linked to how its training prompts were generated?
questions.answer: SAM learned from point and box prompts simulated from masks, so those are the inputs it understands at inference time.
questions.explanation: Check that you link the training recipe (this page) to the prompting sections (pp.347, 351).

questions.question: Why not simply resize the fruit image to 1024 × 1024?
options: It would distort the aspect ratio, because the image isn't square
It would change the number of color channels
questions.answer: It would distort the aspect ratio, because the image isn't square
questions.explanation: The page says so directly. Speed is not the issue, SAM does expect square 1024 × 1024 input, and resizing never changes the channel count.

questions.question: An image is 600 pixels tall and 800 pixels wide. After resize-and-pad to 1024 × 1024, what is the size of the resized content, and how many padding rows are added in total?
questions.answer: Scale $s = 1024/800 = 1.28$: content is 768 × 1024 (H × W); $1024 - 768 = 256$ padding rows in total.
questions.explanation: The longest side (width) becomes 1024; height scales by the same factor; only the height gets padded. (In Keras the 256 rows are split 128/128.)

questions.question: Which argument of `keras.ops.image.resize()` gives aspect-ratio-preserving resizing with padding?
questions.answer: `pad_to_aspect_ratio=True`
questions.explanation: Used in `resize_and_pad` on the page.

questions.question: List the four display utilities the authors plan to write.
questions.answer: Display images; display segmentation masks overlaid on an image; highlight specific points on an image; display boxes overlaid on an image.
questions.explanation: The bullet list on the page; their code is on p.347.

questions.question: Why do all the utilities take a Matplotlib axis object `ax` instead of creating their own plots?
questions.answer: So they can all draw on the same figure, layering the image, mask, points and boxes on top of each other.
questions.explanation: Stated in the last sentence on the page.

questions.question: After `resize_and_pad`, why is it important to specify prompt points in the coordinates of `image` rather than of `image_array`?
questions.answer: The model sees `image` (scaled and padded); a point from the original image would land on a different location unless it is scaled by $s$ and shifted by the padding offset.
questions.explanation: Inference from the preprocessing; the point prompts on p.347–348 are drawn on and passed with `image`.

questions.question: Could you implement resize-and-pad by hand (compute the scale, resize, pad) without `pad_to_aspect_ratio`?
questions.answer: Yes: s = 1024 / max(H, W); resize to (round(sH), round(sW)); pad the short side with zeros up to 1024.
questions.explanation: Compare with the formula in the math section.

questions.question: What does a point labeled 0 mean in a SAM point prompt?
options: The point is the first object to segment
The point belongs to the background and should be excluded
The point marks class 0 of a fixed label set
questions.answer: The point belongs to the background and should be excluded
questions.explanation: The page defines 1 as foreground and 0 as background (what to exclude). The label isn't an index or a class, and it isn't ignored.

questions.question: What are the shapes of `input_point` and `input_label` in the test code, and what do they contain?
questions.answer: `input_point` is (1, 2), holding one point (x = 580, y = 450); `input_label` is (1,), holding [1] (foreground).
questions.explanation: From the second listing and its callouts.

questions.question: In `show_mask`, a pixel has mask value 1. What RGBA value does `mask_image` hold there, and what about a pixel with mask value 0?
questions.explanation: The mask is multiplied by the RGBA color through broadcasting.

questions.question: `show_box` is called with `np.array([[100, 50, 300, 250]])`. What width and height does it pass to `plt.Rectangle`?
questions.explanation: After flattening, w = box[2] - box[0] = 300 - 100 = 200 and h = box[3] - box[1] = 250 - 50 = 200. The other options use raw coordinates instead of differences.

questions.question: When might you pass several labeled points instead of one, and how would you label them?
questions.answer: In ambiguous cases, such as a point that could mean a part, an object or a group. Add points labeled 1 on regions that must be included and points labeled 0 on regions that must be excluded.
questions.explanation: The page recommends multiple labeled points to refine the definition of what should be included and excluded.

questions.question: Why do the helper calls use `plt.gca()`?
questions.answer: So that `show_image` and `show_points` draw on the same current Axes, layering the point on top of the image.
questions.explanation: All utilities take an `ax` so they can write to the same figure (p.346). `gca` returns the current Axes.

questions.question: Can you write, from memory, a prompt with two foreground points and one background point, and say what shape each array has?
questions.answer: `np.array([[x1, y1], [x2, y2], [x3, y3]])` with shape (3, 2), and `np.array([1, 1, 0])` with shape (3,).
questions.explanation: This generalizes the single-point example on the page.

questions.question: What does the shape (1, 4, 256, 256) of outputs["masks"] mean?
options: 4 images in the batch, each with a single 256 × 256 mask
questions.answer: 1 batch element, 4 candidate masks, each 256 × 256
questions.explanation: The page states the field contains four 256 × 256 candidate masks; the leading 1 is the batch axis added with expand_dims. There are no color channels in a mask, SAM gives no classes, and only one image was passed.

questions.question: Why is each input wrapped in ops.expand_dims(..., axis=0)?
questions.answer: To add a batch axis of size 1, because the model processes batches of images and prompts.
questions.explanation: image (1024,1024,3) → (1,1024,1024,3); points (1,2) → (1,1,2); labels (1,) → (1,1). The output keeps that batch axis, hence the [0] in get_mask.

questions.question: Why does get_mask call resize_and_pad on the mask instead of overlaying the 256 × 256 mask directly?
questions.answer: The mask is at a quarter of the input resolution; resizing it to 1024 × 1024 puts it in the same coordinate frame as the padded image so pixel positions line up.
questions.explanation: The image shown in the figures is the 1024 × 1024 padded output of resize_and_pad (p.346). A 256 × 256 mask drawn on it would cover only the top-left quarter. Using the same function guarantees identical framing; padding is a no-op because the mask is square.

questions.question: A candidate mask has 1,200 pixels, the true object has 1,000 pixels, and they overlap on 900 pixels. What IoU should an ideal iou_pred head report?
questions.explanation: IoU = intersection / union and union = |A| + |B| − |A∩B| (p.340).

questions.question: Why does get_mask threshold at 0.0?
options: Because mask values are probabilities and 0.0 is the minimum
Because the values behave like logits, and logit > 0 corresponds to probability > 0.5
Because Matplotlib cannot display negative values
questions.answer: Because the values behave like logits, and logit > 0 corresponds to probability > 0.5
questions.explanation: With probabilities, thresholding at 0 would include almost every pixel. The padding value and Matplotlib are unrelated to the decision boundary. (The logit interpretation is an explanation beyond the book's text.)

questions.question: Why would a promptable segmentation model return several candidate masks rather than one?
questions.answer: A single point is ambiguous: it can belong to nested objects or parts. Returning several masks with quality scores lets the user or a program pick the intended one.
questions.explanation: The book shows this on p.350-351, where alternatives for the banana prompt include both bananas.

questions.question: Without looking, can you write get_mask and state the shape after each line?
questions.explanation: If you can reproduce this, you can adapt SAM's output to any display or downstream use.

questions.question: What changes between the peach example and the banana example?
questions.answer: Only the prompt point coordinates
questions.explanation: The banana listing reuses the same image, model, predict call, get_mask and plotting code; only input_point changes from (580, 450) to (300, 550). The label stays 1.

questions.question: What does `plt.gca()` return and why is it passed to every helper?
questions.answer: The current Matplotlib axis; passing the same axis lets image, mask and points be drawn on top of each other in one plot.
questions.explanation: The helpers on p.347 all take an `ax` argument so they can write to the same figure.

questions.question: Why is the banana a more interesting test of SAM than the peach?
questions.answer: The two bananas touch and look alike, so a point on one could mean 'this banana' or 'the bananas'; this ambiguity is what the multiple candidate masks address.
questions.explanation: On p.350-351 the alternative masks show the model offering both interpretations.

questions.question: If you accidentally wrote input_point = np.array([[550, 300]]), where would the point land?
options: On the same banana, since order does not matter
Higher up and further right, around the bowl and fruit
questions.answer: Higher up and further right, around the bowl and fruit
questions.explanation: x = 550 is right of center and y = 300 is in the upper half, which in Figure 11.11 is the bowl region near the yellow fruit (the "mango" of p.351). It is inside the image, and well above the bottom padding.

questions.question: Why does the banana listing call get_mask with index=0, and what would index=3 give?
questions.answer: index=0 takes the first candidate; index=3 would take the last of the four alternative masks, which may represent a different granularity of the object.
questions.explanation: outputs["masks"] holds four candidates (p.348). The next page plots indices 1-3.

questions.question: Can you predict what a point placed on the yellow fruit at the top of the bowl (the mango of p.351) would produce, and write the code for it?
questions.answer: Change input_point to a coordinate on that fruit (for example around (650, 300), inside the p.351 box) and rerun the same listing; the first mask should cover it.
questions.explanation: Tests whether you understood that only the prompt changes. The coordinate is an estimate from the figure.

questions.question: Which candidate indices does `outputs["masks"][0][1:]` contain?
questions.explanation: [0] removes the batch axis leaving 4 candidates; [1:] starts at index 1 and runs to the end. 0,1,2 would be [:3]; the others drop candidates.

questions.question: In Figure 11.13, which masks include both bananas?
questions.answer: Mask 2 and Mask 3.
questions.explanation: Mask 1 covers only the second banana, like Figure 11.12; the other two extend to the first banana (confirmed by the text on p.351).

questions.question: Why does it make sense for SAM to return several masks for one point?
questions.answer: A point does not specify the extent of the intended object; it may refer to a part, an object, or a group. Several candidates cover these interpretations.
questions.explanation: The banana prompt is the book's example: one banana or both are both plausible.

questions.question: What would happen if `index=i + 1` were changed to `index=i`?
options: Nothing; the same masks are plotted
Masks 0, 1, 2 would be plotted, so candidate 3 is never shown
questions.answer: Masks 0, 1, 2 would be plotted, so candidate 3 is never shown
questions.explanation: i runs 0-2. index=i selects candidates 0-2, all valid indices, so no error, but the titles would be off by one and candidate 3 skipped.

questions.question: Besides looking at alternative masks, how could you make SAM segment both bananas, or only one, more reliably?
questions.answer: Add more labeled points: a foreground point on the first banana to include it, or a background point (label 0) on it to exclude it. A box prompt (p.351) is another option.
questions.explanation: p.347 describes passing multiple labeled points to refine what is included and excluded.

questions.question: Can you explain why the loop variable `mask` from enumerate is never actually used?
questions.answer: Line 6 reassigns `mask` to get_mask(outputs, index=i + 1) before it is read, so only i matters.
questions.explanation: Recognising this helps you read and simplify example code.

questions.question: How is a box prompt specified in this section?
options: Center (x, y) plus width and height
A binary mask of the box region
questions.answer: Top-left and bottom-right corner coordinates
questions.explanation: The text says boxes are passed via the coordinates of their top-left and bottom-right corners. Center/size and corner/size are other conventions; four corners are redundant for an axis-aligned box; a mask is a different kind of prompt.

questions.question: Compute the width, height and area of input_box = [[520, 180], [770, 420]].
questions.explanation: w = x1 − x0 = 770 − 520; h = y1 − y0 = 420 − 180, as show_box computes (p.347).

questions.question: Why is a box prompt usually less ambiguous than a single point prompt?
questions.answer: It specifies the extent of the object as well as its location, ruling out interpretations much larger or smaller than the box.
questions.explanation: With the banana point, SAM proposed both one-banana and two-banana masks (p.350-351); a box around one banana would exclude the second.

questions.question: What does the first sentence on this page conclude about the banana prompt?
questions.answer: An alternative segmentation found by the model includes both bananas.
questions.explanation: It refers to Masks 2 and 3 in Figure 11.13 (p.350).

questions.question: If you passed input_box = [[770, 420], [520, 180]] to show_box, what would happen?
options: It computes negative width and height
It draws a box around the whole image
questions.answer: It computes negative width and height
questions.explanation: show_box takes box[2] − box[0] = 520 − 770 = −250 and similarly −240. Matplotlib may still draw a rectangle anchored at the other corner, but the convention is broken and SAM itself expects the documented order; it is not the 'same box' by construction, and no error is raised.

questions.question: How might the box prompts of this section connect to the next chapter?
questions.answer: Chapter 12 is about object detectors, which output bounding boxes; such boxes could be fed to SAM as prompts to obtain masks.
questions.explanation: The chaining idea is an inference; the book only states that detection is about drawing bounding boxes (p.353).

questions.question: Can you draw (on paper) the 1024 × 1024 frame with the mango box and label its corners?
questions.answer: Box from x 520-770, y 180-420, in the upper right of the image, inside the bowl.
questions.explanation: Practising coordinate conventions avoids the common x/y and corner-order mistakes.

questions.question: What is the shape of the "boxes" input after ops.expand_dims(input_box, axis=(0, 1))?
questions.explanation: input_box is (2, 2); inserting size-1 axes at positions 0 and 1 gives (1, 1, 2, 2). (1, 2, 2) would be axis=0 only; (1, 4) would require flattening.

questions.question: Which input keys are passed to SAM for the box prompt?
questions.answer: "images" and "boxes".
questions.explanation: Unlike the point prompt (p.348), no "points" or "labels" are given.

questions.question: In Figure 11.15, the box includes parts of the apples, yet the mask does not. Why?
questions.answer: The box only indicates the approximate location and size of the target; SAM segments the single object the box frames, the mango, at pixel precision.
questions.explanation: SAM was trained with boxes drawn around one object's mask (p.345), so it learned to return that object, not everything in the box.

questions.question: Why does the book say SAM is useful for creating segmentation datasets?
questions.answer: Producing masks by hand is slow; SAM turns each object into a one-click or one-box task, with humans only correcting errors.
questions.explanation: Mask labels are much more costly than boxes (p.354), and SA-1B itself was built this way (p.343).

questions.question: According to the summary, which layer pair is used to build a segmentation model from scratch?
options: Strided Conv2D layers followed by Conv2DTranspose layers
questions.answer: Strided Conv2D layers followed by Conv2DTranspose layers
questions.explanation: The second summary bullet says exactly this. The other options are not the chapter's architecture.

questions.question: The summary says SAM supports text prompting. Is that supported by what the chapter showed?
questions.answer: No. The chapter explains and demonstrates only point and box prompts; text prompting is not covered.
questions.explanation: p.344 says the prompt can be a point or a box; p.347 lists only those two. Read the summary claim critically.

questions.question: Can you list, from memory, the two prompt types you used with SAM and the input keys each needs?
questions.answer: Point: images, points (1,1,2), labels (1,1). Box: images, boxes (1,1,2,2).
questions.explanation: Consolidates 11.3.4 and 11.3.5.
